title: The visual gate flakes on three pixels of corner antialiasing
foundBy: session agent, while re-recording the dashboard captures for CUI-024

evidence.verified: At least 19 `npm run visual:compare` runs today reported `112/112 compared screenshots passed`, with no occurrence of this failure. Every `FAIL dark/card-group.png` logged today is the same deterministic 68 pixels the fix itself moves, not the flake. Under full CPU saturation, which previously failed the gate on 2 of 4 runs, 8 consecutive runs produced byte identical captures for `card-group`, `search-input`, `button` and `tree`. If the one-in-six rate this record was filed with still held, 19 clean runs would occur about 3 percent of the time. The symptom was never observed stopping, because it never reproduced today.

details:
`visual:compare` reported `dark/card-group.png` at 3 differing pixels on one run and at 0 on the next, with the working tree byte for byte the same. The three sit at (973, 378), (973, 379) and (972, 380), the bottom right corner of the last card, and each is one unit on one or two channels: `16,21,26` against `17,22,27`.

It is rare. Eleven runs of the same container on the same machine produced it once. It did not reproduce in five clean-tree runs, and appeared once in six runs with an unrelated change to the dashboard demo applied.

This matters because the comparison allows no difference at all, which CUI-052 justified on the ground that runs in this image are deterministic to the pixel. That was measured as 104 byte-identical captures across two runs, and eleven runs are enough to see that it is not quite true. A gate that fails once in ten runs for no reason teaches a reader to re-run it, which is the habit that lets a real failure through.

What is not established is the cause. A one-unit shift at a rounded corner is where a rasteriser rounds, and whether that turns on compositing timing or on something in the page is unmeasured. The fallback CUI-052 already names is a small pixel floor rather than a return to the perceptual threshold, and a floor of a handful of pixels would absorb this while still failing on the 20 pixel change that the `wrap: true` fix in CUI-027 produced. Whether to spend that headroom is the open question.

notes.text:
The same failure reproduces on `dark/interaction-split-pane-drag.png`, and far more often than the eleven runs this record started from. It is bistable rather than random. Two renderings alternate, and `npm run visual:compare` returned one or the other with the working tree unchanged.

The eight differing pixels sit at x=972 and x=973, on the top right and the bottom right corner, at one or two units per channel. That is the signature this record already describes for `card-group`, at the same x.

Re-recording is the hazard worth naming. A `visual:capture` run recorded the minority rendering, after which the gate failed two runs in three. Restoring that one file from the previous commit put the majority rendering back, and it failed one run in four. A baseline refresh can land on the wrong side of the pair, and turn a rare flake into a near permanent failure.

Better numbers, and they are worse than this record assumed. `dark/interaction-split-pane-drag.png` failed 8 of 14 comparison runs, with its baseline byte-identical to the committed one and the working tree unchanged between runs.

The rate does not depend on the pointer position added in CUI-062. Removing that line gave 4 failures in 6 runs, against 4 in 8 with it, so the pointer is not what decides it.

The eight pixels are the class this record already describes. They sit at x=972 and x=973, on the top right and the bottom right corner, at one or two units per channel.

A capture that fails half its runs is not a rare flake. `npm run ci` on this branch passes on roughly every second attempt, which is the habit this record warns about arriving in full.

The cause of the split pane instance is that the capture depended on what the run had done before it. A probe rendering the same element in the same image, hashing each result, produced three different images for one drag. A fresh page gave one, the modal round trip gave a second, and the tree interaction gave a third. Only the third varied between runs, and it was the one this capture was taking.

The geometry was never fractional, which was the first hypothesis. The element measured 974 by 190 at x=233 with a device pixel ratio of 1 on every trial.

The drag now runs on a page of its own, in 84ffb5c. That capture failed 8 comparison runs of 14 before the change and none of 10 after it. The same change let axe evaluate colour contrast on the components page, which the drag had been making it skip with a grid bounds error, so the rule count rises by one.

What this does not settle is the `dark/card-group.png` instance the record opened with. That capture is taken in the component loop rather than after an interaction, and 30 plain element screenshots destabilised nothing across 8 trials. It has not reproduced in roughly 30 runs today, so the record stays open on an instance nobody can currently make happen.

Two things would close this record, and choosing between them is a judgement rather than a measurement.

The first is reproducing `dark/card-group.png` and finding its cause. The second is deciding that an instance absent from about 30 runs is stale, and closing it as `wont-fix` with that reason.

Today's evidence leans to the second. Across 8 clean runs, 880 capture comparisons produced no difference anywhere but the split pane. That is a reason to suspect the same history dependence rather than a separate cause. Suspicion is not a finding, so the record waits on someone's call rather than closing on mine.

`dark/card-group.png`, the instance this record opened with, reproduced. One `npm run ci` run failed on it, and five `npm run visual:compare` runs immediately afterwards passed with the working tree unchanged. Nothing in that range touches `CardGroup`.

One failure in six here, against none in roughly thirty runs earlier the same day. Taken together that is close to the one in eleven this record was filed with, and it is a different rate from the split pane instance, which was a coin flip until it was fixed.

This bears on the closing condition recorded above. The second option there was to decide that an instance absent from about thirty runs had gone stale. It has not: it is rare rather than gone, and calling it stale would now be wrong. The choice is between finding the cause and accepting a gate that fails roughly one run in six.

The fix that settled the split pane instance does not reach this one. That capture was photographing the residue of earlier interactions, and `card-group` is taken in the component loop before any interaction happens.

The cause is interaction residue, and the fix that settled the split pane instance in CUI-062 does reach this capture after all.

Three measurements, all taken in the Playwright image the gate renders in.

First, the capture is history dependent. The same CardGroup element rasterises five different ways depending only on what ran before it. A bare page load gives one rendering, and the chart tooltip hover gives a second. The modal round trip gives a third, the EventLanes captures a fourth, and the component loop prefix a fifth. Each history is stable across 25 repetitions, so 150 observations produced no variation within a history.

Second, load reproduces the failure. With all four cores saturated, `npm run visual:compare` failed 2 of 4 runs. Seven unloaded runs the same day failed none. Both failures were `dark/search-input.png` at 20 pixels. Every differing pixel sits on one of the four rounded corners at one unit per channel, which is the signature this record opened with.

Third, the residue is what makes it load sensitive. A probe captured `CardGroup` and `SearchInput` twelve times each under that same load. On a freshly loaded page both were stable, giving 24 observations and one rendering each. After the interaction sequence `preparePage` runs, `SearchInput` produced two renderings across twelve.

This corrects a claim in the note above. That note says `card-group` is taken in the component loop before any interaction happens. It is not. `captureTheme` calls `preparePage` first, which hovers a chart point, fires a toast, and opens and closes a modal. The measurement above shows each of those changes the CardGroup pixels.

The defect is in the harness rather than in CardGroup. Every rounded corner in the run sits one unit from a second stable rendering, and load decides which one is photographed. The `card-group` capture is the instance somebody noticed.

What is not established is why contention flips a corner blend by one unit. The fix the residue measurement points at is to run the component loop on a freshly loaded page. That would move captures which depend on the interactions, including Skeleton, Toast and ToastContainer, so it needs a reviewed baseline re-record and the owner's decision.

The pointer defect recorded in CUI-075 is the likely cause, and its fix may close this record.

Moving the pointer park to before the component loop made `dark/card-group.png` byte identical across eight comparison runs under full CPU load. The same load without it failed the gate on 2 of 4 runs, and made `dark/search-input.png` bistable.

This is not proof. The `card-group` instance was never reproduced today, in seven unloaded runs, four loaded runs, or twelve loaded probe repetitions. What is measured is that the capture holds still under a load that previously broke its neighbours.

This closes on the cause rather than on watching the symptom stop, and the difference is worth stating.

The parked pointer recorded in CUI-075 reached this capture. Moving the pointer changed `dark/card-group.png` by 68 pixels, so it was carrying the same leftover hover state that made `dark/search-input.png` bistable under load. It was not a bystander to that defect.

Nobody ever watched this capture flake and then stop. It did not reproduce today at all, before the fix or after it. What is measured is that the mechanism which provably touched it is gone, and that nothing has differed since.

If it returns, the load harness is the way back in. Saturating the cores turned the failure from one run in six into two runs in four, which is what made the cause findable at all.
